learning_objective: 🎯 Master circuits where electricity constantly changes direction, decipher phasor diagrams, and learn how transformers power the world!

main_concepts.concept_title: 〰️ AC vs DC and RMS Values
main_concepts.simple_explanation: Direct Current (DC) flows one way, but Alternating Current (AC) sloshes back and forth smoothly like a sine wave. Because AC averages to zero over a full cycle, we use 'RMS' (Root Mean Square) values to measure its effective voltage and current.

In AC circuits, voltage and current don't always peak at the same time; one might 'lead' or 'lag' the other. We use rotating vectors called Phasors to easily draw and calculate these phase differences.
When an Inductor (L), Capacitor (C), and Resistor (R) are all connected in series to AC, they collectively oppose the current. This total combined opposition is called Impedance ($Z$).

At a very specific frequency, the opposition from the inductor exactly cancels out the opposition from the capacitor ($X_L = X_C$). The impedance becomes minimum, and the current spikes to its maximum. This is how you tune a radio!

A device that uses mutual induction to step-up (increase) or step-down (decrease) AC voltages. High voltage is used to transmit power across the country to reduce energy loss, then stepped down safely for your home.

fun_activity.title: 📻 The Radio Tuner
fun_activity.instructions: Turn the dial on an old FM/AM radio. You are actually physically turning a variable capacitor inside! When its capacitance perfectly matches the circuit's inductance for a specific station's frequency, the circuit reaches 'Resonance' and plays that station clearly.

exam_tips: 📌 Always draw the Phasor Diagram for LCR circuits; examiners give heavy weightage to clear, labeled diagrams.
📌 Remember the phrase 'ELI the ICE man': Voltage leads Current in an Inductor (ELI), and Current leads Voltage in a Capacitor (ICE).
📌 When asked about transformer losses, list all four: Copper loss (heat in wires), Iron loss (eddy currents in core), Flux leakage, and Hysteresis loss.
quick_recap: ⭐ The AC voltage coming into your house (220V) is an RMS value, meaning the actual peak voltage is around 311V!
⭐ In a purely resistive circuit, voltage and current are perfectly in phase.
⭐ Transformers ONLY work with AC. If you connect a transformer to a DC battery, it will not step up/down the voltage and might burn out.
